headline: Hawkish Fed Hold Keeps a December Hike in View
tileReason: The daily 30-year average edged up to 7.35% after the Fed held rates but left the door open to a December hike; this morning's in-line inflation data and a tech selloff are steadying bonds.
takeaway: Mortgage rates barely moved on Fed day. The daily 30-year average rose 0.02% to 7.35% on Wednesday, still only a few hundredths above last week's one-month low. The Federal Reserve (the Fed, the central bank) held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4.00%, as expected, but two officials voted for a hike, and the statement upgraded the economy from "solid" to "strong." Chair Warsh said inflation remains elevated and declined to signal what comes next. Markets read that as a hawkish hold, meaning one that leans toward higher rates: futures now put the odds of a December hike at roughly 83% to 88%, up from about 78% before the meeting. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, closed near 5.05% Wednesday, up about 0.05%. This morning brought a mixed picture. September PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred gauge) came in exactly as forecast, 3.6% over the past year and 3.1% for the core measure that leaves out food and energy, so there was no fresh shock. Economic growth was stronger than expected, at a 3.4% yearly pace for the third quarter. Meanwhile Alphabet's disappointing earnings are dragging on tech stocks, which tends to send money into bonds, and oil is down about 1% on renewed U.S.-Iran diplomacy. The net result: the 10-year yield has slipped back to about 5.00%, which points to steady to slightly better lender pricing today. Freddie Mac's weekly survey comes out at noon ET. Over the next month the odds look close to balanced, with a slight lean toward rates staying about where they are.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via KuCoin News (Oct 29), Daily Wrap (Oct 28 close) and Admiral Markets (Oct 28); Bloomberg futures data via Yahoo Finance (Oct 28)
fedOdds.note: After Wednesday's hawkish hold, CME FedWatch odds of a quarter-point hike at the Dec 9 meeting rose to about 86% to 88% Wednesday (Daily Wrap 86.0%, Admiral Markets 87.5%) and were about 83% Thursday morning (KuCoin News). Sources differ on the pre-meeting level: about 78% (Daily Wrap, KuCoin) versus 73% (Admiral Markets). Bloomberg futures data showed about 85%.

drivers.title: Hawkish Fed hold keeps a December hike in play
drivers.text: The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4.00% Wednesday, but two officials dissented in favor of a hike and the statement called the economy's growth "strong" rather than "solid." Chair Warsh said inflation remains elevated and wouldn't rule anything out. Investors now see roughly an 83% to 88% chance of a hike in December, which keeps a floor under bond yields. The 10-year yield rose about 0.05% to near 5.05% Wednesday, though mortgage rates rose only 0.02% because lenders had already priced in most of the news.

drivers.title: Inflation in line, growth stronger than expected
drivers.text: September's PCE inflation matched forecasts at 3.6% for the year, with the core measure (no food or energy) at 3.1%, up from 3.0% in August. No surprise meant no big move, but inflation is still well above the Fed's 2% goal. Third-quarter growth came in at a 3.4% yearly pace, faster than the roughly 3.1% to 3.2% forecasters expected. A strong economy and sticky inflation make a December hike more likely, which tends to hold mortgage rates up.

drivers.title: Alphabet slide revives tech worries
drivers.text: Alphabet shares fell sharply after its earnings missed forecasts and its cash flow turned negative on heavy AI spending, and Nasdaq futures are down about 1% this morning. When stocks wobble, investors tend to move money into bonds, which pushes yields and mortgage rates down. That's a big reason the 10-year yield has slipped back to about 5.00% this morning despite the strong growth number.

drivers.title: Oil eases on renewed U.S.-Iran diplomacy
drivers.text: Brent crude is down about 1% this morning to roughly $114 a barrel after reports of a U.S. letter seeking to revive talks with Iran and a Qatari draft proposal. Lower oil eases inflation worries a little, which helps bonds. Continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and talk of possible U.S. strikes after the midterms are limiting the decline.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates are still unusually far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming 30-year index is running about 2.20% above the 10-year Treasury yield (as of Oct 26), versus a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra cushion means mortgage rates have room to improve if markets calm down, even without a further drop in Treasury yields.

outlook.basis: It's close to a coin flip, with a slight lean toward rates staying about where they are and a small tilt toward higher rather than lower after the Fed's hawkish tone. Working against borrowers: a December Fed hike now looks very likely, inflation is still running well above target, growth is strong, and oil remains above $110. Working in their favor: tech stocks are shaky again, which can send money into bonds quickly; U.S.-Iran diplomacy is still alive; and mortgage rates are unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.2% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), leaving room to improve. Big swing events: Friday's wage data, the November 3 midterm elections, the November 6 jobs report, the November 10 CPI report, and any escalation in the Gulf.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average is about 7.35%, close to a one-month low and down from roughly 7.5% in early October. The Fed kept a December hike on the table, and the jobs and inflation reports in early November could bring bigger swings than usual, so it's worth asking your lender how locking, a float-down option, or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Buyers are still stretched at rates above 7%, and the Fed's tone suggests relief may be slow to come. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: The Fed held rates steady but kept a December hike in play; mortgage rates are steady around 7.35%, near a one-month low.
